## The record with a blank where the important field should be

Your systems administrator is doing something routine: adding the eQMS (electronic
quality-management system) to the CMDB (configuration management database) — the record of
every system IT runs, kept current so anyone can see what exists and what depends on what. He
pulls up the entry he's drafted. Name, a version number, "owned by: IT," a short description.
Clean, fast, exactly the kind of record he's built hundreds of times for hundreds of other
systems.

Your Quality Analyst (QA) is reading over his shoulder, because the eQMS is hers as much as his
— it's where CAPA (corrective and preventive action) records, document control, and
internal-audit logs live for all three of Lakeshore's sites. She asks one question: "Where does
it say whether this thing is actually qualified to run? What cycle is it on?"

He checks the template. There's no field for that. There's never been a field for that — every
other system in the CMDB is a laptop, a network switch, a ticketing tool, nothing anyone outside
IT has ever asked to see a qualification status on. "I can add a note," he offers. "Not the same
thing as a real field," she says, "and not something I'd want to explain to an assessor who asks
why the one system holding our audit trail doesn't carry the one piece of information that tells
her it's trustworthy."

Nobody did anything wrong here. The CMDB did exactly what a CMDB is built to do. It just was
never built to answer the question your QA just asked — and that gap, not any single mistake, is
this lesson's actual subject.

## Why this matters — and the ITSM bridges you already own

Here's the failure this gap can produce, and it's worth naming before any framework enters the
room: a system holds the evidence an AABB (Association for the Advancement of Blood &
Biotherapies) assessor or an FDA investigator will actually rely on, and nothing in its own
IT-side record says whether that system has ever been proven fit to do the job. Not because
anyone hid it — because the record IT already keeps was never designed to ask. A CMDB entry that
can tell you a system's version but not its qualification status is a record built for a
different question than the one a regulated environment actually needs answered.

You already own three ITSM (IT service management) concepts that sit exactly where this gap
lives, and this lesson's whole job is giving each one a working AABB counterpart.

**The CMDB** you just watched your administrator populate: a record of configuration items
(CIs — a system, a component, a piece of infrastructure) and the relationships between them, kept
current so anyone can answer "what exists, what version, what does it depend on, what depends on
it." **The service catalog**: a listing of what IT actually offers, to whom, at what service
level — the artifact a site operations lead or a Quality director reads to find out what a given
service actually promises. **Continual improvement**: a standing register of improvement ideas,
each with an owner and a status, reviewed periodically so a good idea from a retrospective doesn't
simply evaporate once the meeting ends.

All three already have a direct, working counterpart inside AABB's own framework — not identical,
the same honest caveat this course has carried since module 1, but close enough, and different
enough, to be worth mapping precisely rather than gesturing at. CMDB maps onto AABB's own
**equipment and validated-system inventory** concept. Service catalog maps onto a **quality
system's own defined scope**. Continual improvement maps onto AABB's own **process-improvement**
discipline. Build all three concretely, using the eQMS as the live example, and you'll have this
course's first real artifact — the same CMDB entry and service-catalog entry module 4 picks back
up and finishes.

## A note on citations: there isn't a new one here

This module introduces no new regulatory source, the same discipline the plan for this course set
from the start. `sources/aabb/qse-framework.md` names AABB's Quality System Essentials (QSEs) as a
ten-element taxonomy — themes and titles only, never Standards text, never a standard number. Two
of those ten do real work below: **QSE 3, Equipment** — covering equipment selection,
qualification (in IQ/OQ/PQ-style language — installation, operational, and performance
qualification, the same vocabulary `csv-and-becs` built out in full for BECS), monitoring, and
maintenance, and stated explicitly, in AABB's own framework, to include IT systems — and **QSE 9,
Process Improvement** — titled "Process Improvement Through Corrective and Preventive Action" in
an older AABB template, per that same source file's own note. Both are named and themed only,
exactly the discipline `aabb-qse-framework` modeled first. ITIL's own vocabulary — CMDB, service
catalog, continual improvement — is never cited to a specific AXELOS/PeopleCert publication
anywhere in this curriculum. It's your professional background, used as a bridge, not a standard
anyone is auditing Lakeshore against.

## Crosswalk 1: CMDB ↔ equipment and validated-system inventory

Line up what each record actually holds, field for field.

| A CMDB's CI record holds | An AABB-governed equipment/validated-system inventory entry holds | What's the same | What's genuinely different |
|---|---|---|---|
| What it is (name, type, description) | What it is | Both start with plain identification. Nothing differs here. | — |
| Its version | Its qualification status — installed, operationally qualified, performance qualified, due for revalidation | Both track a single current state for the item. | This is the real gap, and it's the one your QA just caught. A CMDB's "version" field answers *what build is running*. It does not, by default ITIL practice, answer *has anyone proven this build actually works correctly* — that second question simply isn't part of what a CMDB is built to ask. |
| Its dependencies and relationships (what it runs on, what talks to it) | What it depends on and feeds, as part of its qualified, validated operation | Both exist to answer "if this breaks, what else breaks with it." | Lakeshore's version ties each dependency back to a quality-relevant consequence — the same connection `change-control-for-regulated-systems` already drew for the inventory-system patch in module 1 — where a CMDB's dependency map, on its own, is relationship data without that consequence attached. |
| Who owns it | Who owns it, for maintenance *and* for the qualification record itself | Both name an accountable owner. | AABB's version can require two names doing different jobs — an IT owner for the system itself, a quality owner for the record proving it's qualified — where a CMDB typically names one. |

Here's the honest version of that gap, stated plainly rather than softened: **a CMDB entry, in
plain ITIL practice, does not carry a required qualification or validation-status field.** Nothing
about ITIL's own discipline demands one, because most of what a CMDB tracks — a laptop, a switch,
a ticketing tool — was never going to be qualified in the first place. An AABB-governed equipment
or system inventory entry is built around the opposite assumption: the qualification status *is*
the record's whole point, because QSE 3 explicitly extends equipment qualification to IT systems,
not just lab instruments and centrifuges. A CMDB and a validated-system inventory are structurally
similar — identity, current state, dependencies, owner — and they're answering genuinely different
questions about that state.

BECS (Blood Establishment Computer Software) already lives on the stricter side of that line.
`csv-and-becs` built its own full validation lifecycle — a validation plan, executed IQ/OQ/PQ
evidence, a traceability matrix, and a standing periodic-review cycle that reopens the question
every time a patch or a configuration change lands, all reference-only here, not redeveloped. The
eQMS, now that you're looking at it this way, sits on that same side of the line, even though
nobody built it a BECS-style validation package from day one. It holds the evidence an assessor
relies on; QSE 3's own scope reaches IT systems explicitly; the honest conclusion is that a bare
CMDB entry was never going to be enough for this particular system; it needs the qualification
field a validated-system inventory assumes by default.

### The eQMS's own CMDB entry — this course's first real artifact

Here's the draft entry, built concretely, carried forward to module 4.

| Field | This entry |
|---|---|
| **CI name** | eQMS (electronic quality-management system) |
| **CI type** | Application |
| **Current version** | Current production release |
| **Owner (system)** | Systems administrator, on behalf of IT |
| **In production at** | Lakeshore's central site, Brookfield, and Fairview |
| **Depends on** | The central identity/access system (authentication for all eQMS accounts across all three sites); each site's local network infrastructure; the underlying storage/backup system the eQMS's records are written to |
| **Feeds / relied on by** | Quality staff at all three sites, for CAPA tracking, document control, and internal-audit logging; site operations leadership, for document-control access |
| **Qualification/validation status** | *Not a standard CMDB field — blank by default, the exact gap your QA caught above* |

That blank last row is the artifact's honest point, not an oversight to quietly fill in. A CI
record this complete on every other field, with nothing at all answering "is it fit to run the
job it's doing," is precisely what a validated-system inventory entry would never allow — and
precisely what module 4 picks up directly, building the field a plain CMDB template never asked
for.

One dependency worth being precise about by its absence: nothing here claims a data interface
between the eQMS and BECS. They're separate systems, serving separate functions, and this course
doesn't invent a connection between them that was never established. The eQMS replaced an older,
BECS-*adjacent* quality-tracking tool, per `risk-frameworks-side-by-side` — "adjacent" is doing
real work in that sentence, and it isn't the same claim as "integrated."

## Crosswalk 2: service catalog ↔ quality-system scope

A service catalog answers three questions about anything IT runs: what does it provide, to whom,
at what level of service. A quality system's own scope statement — the document naming which
processes and activities the quality system actually covers, built on AABB's own framework —
answers a parallel set of questions: what's covered, where, and under what quality commitment.
Same three questions, asked by two different owners, about the same system. That's the whole
crosswalk, and it's worth building both artifacts side by side to see why keeping them in sync
actually matters.

**A plausible, partial service-catalog entry for the eQMS — drafted by IT:**

| Field | Entry |
|---|---|
| **Service** | eQMS |
| **Provides** | CAPA tracking, document control, internal-audit logging |
| **Offered to** | Quality staff and site operations leadership |
| **Offered at** | Central site, Brookfield, and Fairview |
| **Service level** | Business-hours support; next-business-day response for access issues |

**The quality-system scope statement for the same system — owned by Quality:**

> The eQMS is in scope for CAPA management and internal-audit logging across all three sites. The
> eQMS is in scope for document control at the central site and Brookfield. Fairview's
> document-control records remain under the site's existing paper-based process pending
> migration.

Read both again, side by side. The service catalog says document control is offered to all three
sites. The scope statement says document control is only actually in scope for two of them.
That's not a nitpick — it's exactly the kind of inconsistency `fda-and-aabb-in-practice` already
flagged as a real, catchable gap wherever Fairview's paper habit shows up, and this is the same
gap wearing a different artifact's clothes. One of these two documents is wrong, or at least
stale, and nobody can tell which one just by reading either in isolation.

The honest read here, and the one worth saying to your CIO (chief information officer) in one
sentence: **a service catalog and a quality-system scope statement describe the same system from
two different angles, and when they drift apart, it's not a paperwork problem — it's a sign one
of the two owners doesn't actually know what's true in production anymore.** Maybe IT's catalog
entry was drafted optimistically, ahead of Fairview's actual rollout. Maybe it's simply never been
updated since Fairview's migration got delayed. Either way, an assessor reading the scope
statement and a help-desk ticket referencing "document control, all three sites" in the same
review would catch the mismatch in about thirty seconds — and so should you, well before she does.

## Crosswalk 3: continual improvement ↔ process improvement (QSE 9)

ITIL's continual improvement register is a running list: an improvement idea, an owner, a status,
reviewed on some standing cadence so a good suggestion from a retrospective doesn't simply
disappear once the meeting ends. AABB's QSE 9 — Process Improvement, named and themed only, never
quoted — exists for the same underlying reason your QA already knows by a different name: an
identified gap doesn't get to just sit there, untracked, forgotten the moment the room moves on to
something else.

Here's where the two genuinely diverge, and it's worth being precise rather than flattening it.
**ITIL's continual improvement register can hold a purely aspirational or efficiency-driven idea
with no compliance stakes at all** — "this would be nice to streamline" is a perfectly legitimate
register entry on its own terms. **QSE 9's own CAPA-linked process improvement is narrower and
stricter: it's specifically about closing a gap a deviation, an audit, or a nonconformance
actually found** — not just an idea someone had in a meeting. A continual improvement register
with no compliance gate at all would be exactly the wrong instrument for a finding your internal
audit already wrote down; a CAPA would be exactly the wrong instrument for an idea nobody has
actually traced to a real failure yet.

A concrete example, invented fresh for this module, touching nothing any prior course locked:
your systems administrator notices that the eQMS's CAPA-entry screen asks staff to re-key the
same lot or batch number into three separate fields before a new CAPA record saves. Nothing's
broken — every field ends up correct, it's just slower and more annoying than it needs to be.

**As a continual improvement register entry**, that's a clean, honest fit:

| Field | Entry |
|---|---|
| **Idea** | Auto-fill the lot/batch number across the eQMS's CAPA-entry fields after first entry, instead of requiring three separate re-keyed entries |
| **Owner** | Systems administrator |
| **Status** | Proposed, pending a build-effort estimate |
| **Review cadence** | Next quarterly IT service review |

**Would it qualify for QSE 9's own CAPA-linked process?** Not as described above — and saying so
plainly is the actual teaching point. Nothing here traces back to a deviation, an audit finding,
or a nonconformance; it's an efficiency idea with no compliance stakes, exactly the kind of entry
ITIL's own register was built to hold without needing a compliance gate first. That changes the
moment the facts change: if an internal audit instead found that the triple-entry field had
actually caused a real transcription error — a lot number recorded incorrectly on a closed CAPA
record, discovered during a later review — the same underlying issue would need to open as an
actual CAPA, with root cause analysis, corrective and preventive action, and a scheduled
effectiveness check, the full structure `capa-root-cause-to-effectiveness` already built in depth.
The field design is identical in both stories. What decides which register it belongs in isn't the
idea itself — it's whether a real finding, not just a hunch, is driving it.

Lakeshore plausibly needs both registers running, not one replacing the other. A continual
improvement register that only ever held CAPA-worthy findings would quietly lose every genuine
efficiency idea that never rose to that bar — exactly the kind of small, cumulative improvement a
mature ITSM practice exists to capture. A CAPA process that absorbed every minor annoyance,
whether or not a real finding drove it, would dilute the one instrument built to prove a real gap
actually got fixed. Keep them separate, and know, for any given idea, which one it belongs in.

## What an assessor or your CIO would actually look for

Nobody auditing Lakeshore checks whether a system record is called a "CMDB entry" or an
"equipment inventory record." What an AABB assessor actually checks, for any IT system touching a
quality-relevant process, is whether its qualification status is findable, current, and dated —
not whether it lives in a field IT happens to call by a familiar name. What she'd check in a
service catalog or scope statement is whether the two independently describe the same reality;
finding one that promises more than the other admits is itself a finding, regardless of which
document is more up to date. And what she'd check in a continual improvement register is whether
anything in it should have been a CAPA months ago — an idea quietly carrying a real compliance gap
inside language that reads like a nice-to-have.

Your CIO would ask a narrower, faster question: does the eQMS's own record — CMDB, catalog, and
registers together — actually match what's true in production right now, or has the paperwork
drifted from the system while nobody was looking. That's the same question either audience is
asking, in different words.

## Common traps

**"If it's in the CMDB, it's documented — that's good enough."** Documented and qualified are two
different claims. A CMDB entry with a clean version number and a dependency map tells you the
system is tracked. It tells you nothing about whether anyone has actually proven the system works
correctly for the job it's doing, which is the specific question QSE 3 extends to IT systems and
a plain CMDB was never built to answer.

**"The service catalog and the quality-system scope statement are basically the same document
with different headers."** They describe the same system, but they're owned, updated, and relied
on by two different people for two different purposes — which is exactly why they can quietly
drift apart, the way the Fairview document-control line did above. Treating them as interchangeable
is how a stale catalog entry survives for months without anyone catching it.

## What this means for your job

- **Before you accept any CI record for a quality-relevant system as "done," ask the question your
  QA asked above: where's the field that says whether it's actually qualified, and when was that
  status last checked?** If the answer is "there isn't one," that's not a technicality — it's the
  gap this lesson exists to name.
- **Treat a service catalog and a quality-system scope statement as a matched pair that has to be
  reconciled, not two independent documents that happen to describe the same system.** Ask, out
  loud, whether the sites and services named in one actually match the other — the Fairview
  mismatch above is exactly the kind of drift that survives until someone asks.
- **Watch for a continual improvement register quietly carrying a compliance-relevant finding
  dressed up as an efficiency idea.** If an entry traces back to an actual deviation, audit
  finding, or nonconformance, it belongs in a CAPA, with an effectiveness check — not in a backlog
  competing for priority against a nice-to-have.
- **Don't let a legitimate efficiency idea get forced into a CAPA it doesn't need, either.** A CAPA
  with no real finding behind it just adds weight to an instrument that needs to stay credible for
  the findings that actually matter.
- **When you brief your CIO or your exec quality council on the eQMS, use this module's three
  mappings to answer "is this system actually under control" in one breath, in whichever
  vocabulary the room speaks** — but never let the crosswalk itself substitute for the real
  qualification record, the real scope statement, or the real CAPA file an assessor would ask to
  see.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Your systems administrator says, "Every system we run is in the CMDB with a version number, so every system is already properly tracked for AABB purposes." Is that true for the eQMS?

Not on its own. A CMDB entry with a current version number proves the system is tracked and
identified — a real, useful fact. It does not prove the system has been qualified to do the job
it's doing, which is a separate question a plain CMDB field was never built to answer. AABB's QSE
3 (Equipment) explicitly extends equipment qualification to IT systems, and the eQMS holds the
records an assessor relies on — which is exactly why a bare CMDB entry isn't enough for this
particular system, even though it would be perfectly sufficient for a laptop or a network switch.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Does AABB or the FDA require every CMDB entry at Lakeshore to carry a qualification-status field, the way this lesson built one for the eQMS?

No — and this is worth stating as plainly as the parallel question module 1 raised about ITIL
vocabulary. Nothing in AABB's framework or FDA regulation reaches into Lakeshore's general IT
asset records and requires every CI to carry a validation field; most of what IT tracks (a laptop,
a switch, a ticketing tool) was never going to be qualified in the first place, and nothing
requires it to be. What AABB's QSE 3 does require — in substance, not by naming a CMDB field
specifically — is that a system touching a quality-relevant process, like the eQMS, have its
fitness for use established and tracked somewhere. Whether that "somewhere" is a CMDB field, a
separate validated-system inventory, or a dedicated record modeled on BECS's own validation
lifecycle is Lakeshore's own implementation choice, not a specific format any regulation dictates.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: Your Quality Analyst finds the lot/batch triple-entry idea already sitting in IT's continual improvement register, untouched for two quarters. Is that, on its own, a finding she should escalate as a compliance gap?

Not based on what's in the register today. As described, it's a genuine efficiency idea with no
deviation, audit finding, or nonconformance behind it — exactly the kind of entry ITIL's continual
improvement register is built to hold without a compliance gate first, and a slow-moving backlog
item isn't automatically a compliance problem. It becomes one the moment the facts change — if an
audit or investigation ever traces an actual recording error back to that same field design. Until
then, the honest answer is that this entry is doing its job in the register it's already sitting
in, not an overdue CAPA hiding in plain sight.
:::

This module built three honest mappings and one shared artifact: a CMDB entry and a
service-catalog entry for the eQMS, each carrying a gap worth naming rather than smoothing over.
The next module steps back one more layer, crosswalking ITIL's own service-asset-and-configuration
discipline and security management onto the GRC (governance, risk, and compliance) vocabulary
`grc-frameworks-and-risk-management` already built for the eQMS — its RMF (Risk Management
Framework) categorization, its control families, and ISO/IEC 27001's own Annex A domains — using
the eQMS's own already-authorized history as the proof this crosswalk needs, not a new exercise to
build from scratch.
